summary: 39a recounts two parallel 40-year periods: Shimon HaTzaddik's miraculous service (lot always right hand, western lamp continuous, showbread fresh, incense smoke straight) and the 40 years before the Temple's destruction when all these signs reversed, culminating in Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's prophetic rebuke of the self-opening Temple gates.

display.whats: Shimon HaTzaddik served 40 years; four miracles confirmed his righteousness.
display.hint: The lot, the western lamp, the showbread, and the incense smoke all showed miraculous signs during his tenure.
display.title: Shimon HaTzaddik's Forty Years of Miracles

learning.ahaMoment: Forty years of miracles - the lot, the lamp, the bread, and the smoke - each confirmed that Shimon HaTzaddik's service was accepted by God.
learning.memoryAnchor: Four miracles: right-hand lot, western lamp, fresh showbread, straight smoke - all during Shimon HaTzaddik's service.
learning.learnerQuestion: What four miraculous signs marked Shimon HaTzaddik's forty years of service, and why did they matter?
learning.coreTension: Ordinary priestly service could in principle produce the same outward results, lot, lamp, bread, smoke, by chance, yet the baraita treats their unbroken consistency across forty years as proof of something beyond chance.
learning.coreMove: The baraita lists all four signs together, then reports that all four ceased simultaneously upon Shimon HaTzaddik's death, using the abrupt and total reversal to argue the signs were miraculous, tied to him personally, not generic outcomes.

takeaway.text: During Shimon HaTzaddik's forty years, the lot always fell right, the western lamp stayed lit, the showbread stayed fresh, and the incense smoke rose straight, four signs the baraita reads as miraculous confirmation of his service, not coincidence.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may read each sign in isolation as a plausible natural outcome, missing that the baraita's argument rests on all four occurring together for forty straight years and stopping together at his death.

misconceptions.misconception: These were standard, naturally expected results of the Temple service, not miraculous.
misconceptions.correction: The baraita's argument is built on the signs' total reversal immediately after Shimon HaTzaddik's death. If they were standard results of the service itself, they would have continued under his successors. Their simultaneous cessation is the Gemara's evidence that they were tied to him personally, not the routine.

display.title: The Mirror Forty Years: Omens Before the Destruction

learning.ahaMoment: The 40-year countdown to destruction mirrors the 40-year era of Shimon HaTzaddik's miracles - same timeframe, opposite direction.
learning.memoryAnchor: 40 years miracles (Shimon) vs 40 years omens (pre-destruction) - same timeline, inverted meaning.
learning.learnerQuestion: What is the significance of a second forty-year period, this time of decline, appearing in the same baraita tradition?
learning.coreTension: Shimon HaTzaddik's forty years showed favor; the forty years before the destruction showed the same signs in reverse, raising the question of why the Gemara frames decline using the identical timeframe and the identical signs.
learning.coreMove: The baraita reports the lot coming up left, the lamp failing, and the gates opening by themselves, then has Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuke the gates directly, reading their self-opening as the Temple's own admission of its coming fate, fulfilling Zechariah's prophecy.

takeaway.text: Forty years before the destruction, the lot came up left, the western lamp went out, and the Temple gates opened by themselves at night, the same sign-structure as Shimon HaTzaddik's era, inverted, which Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai read as a direct omen of destruction.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may treat these omens as a list of disconnected ill signs rather than recognizing the deliberate parallel structure to the earlier forty years of miracles.

misconceptions.misconception: The 40-year decline signs before the Temple's destruction were universally recognized and led to repentance.
misconceptions.correction: The signs were miraculous and unmistakable, yet they did not produce repentance. The Gemara records them as evidence of what was lost, not as a repentance narrative.

quizSeeds.answer: He rebuked them: 'Heichal, Heichal, why do you alarm yourself? I know your end will be destruction.'

sugyot.finalRuling: 40 years before destruction: lot came left, western lamp went out, gates opened - Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai foretold the end.

rashiTranslations.en: Comes - the one who comes to buy naphtha to measure, since its smell is bad, the seller tells him: measure it yourself. Dulls - it seals and blocks off all wisdom. And you shall become dulled - the word is spelled without an aleph.

They make him impure greatly - they leave him to become impure greatly; and this is what the verse means: do not make yourselves impure through them, but if you do make yourselves impure, in the end you shall become dulled. And you shall sanctify yourselves - a little,
and you shall become holy - greatly: one who comes to become pure,
they assist him.
We shall return to you [the closing formula for the prior chapter]. The appointed one said to them [the new mishnah opens]
Mishnah: He shook the urn - we learned in the chapter above
(37a) that the urn was kept there.
Shook - suddenly, with a shaking and snatching motion.
And he drew up two lots - one in the right hand and one
in the left, with the goats standing one to the right
and one to the left, and he places the lot that comes up in his right hand
on the goat standing to the right. And they answer after him -
when he mentions the divine Name. Gemara: So that he not aim -
so that he not feel around to discern by touch which
lot bears the divine Name and take it specifically in his right hand, since it is a
good sign when it comes up in the right hand. And it was of ordinary [material] -
it was not consecrated. The Torah is considerate,
etc. - as it is said (Leviticus 14), 'and the priest shall command'
'that they empty the house,' etc. Of what is
the Torah considerate? Of earthenware jars, which have
no purification through immersion. If so, it is considerate of
cheap property; all the more so of valuable property. If so,
it is considerate of the property of the afflicted [lepers]; and by an a fortiori
inference, of the property of the righteous. And if
it came up in the deputy's right hand, the head of the father's house
says to the High Priest: speak your word.
Meaning, say your own words: to the Lord, a sin-offering. Since it did not
come up in his hand - that of the High Priest, but it came up in the hand
of the deputy, the High Priest's spirits are dampened; so why should
the deputy tell him? Why is the deputy at his right, etc. -
because he always walks at his right: so they said in the name of
Rabbi Yitzchak HaLevi. But I have heard from my teacher
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yehuda: why is the deputy appointed? So that if
a disqualification should occur, he may serve in his place; but so long as no
disqualification occurs, the deputy performs no service
at all. The strip of crimson wool - combed wool
drawn out in the shape of a tongue and dyed red, and they would tie
it on the head of the goat sent away; and it would
turn white on its own, and this was a sign that the Holy One, Blessed be He, had forgiven
Israel, as it is said (Isaiah 1), 'if
your sins be like scarlet, they shall become white as snow.' And the western lamp
remained lit - after all the other
lamps had gone out; and even though the evening kindling would begin from it,
it was nonetheless the one on which the morning tending
of the lamps would conclude, and this was testimony that the Divine Presence
rests upon Israel, as it is written, 'outside the curtain
of the testimony.' And we say in tractate Shabbat (22b):
'it is testimony to all who come into the world that the Divine Presence
rests upon Israel.' And we say there: what is
this testimony? The western lamp, into which he would pour oil
in the same measure as its fellow lamps, and from it he would begin,
and with it he would conclude. And which is the western lamp?

According to the one who says (Menachot 98b) that the seven lamps were arranged east to west, the 'western lamp' is the second lamp, the one adjacent to the first one on the east, as we learned (Mishnah Tamid 6:1):
one priest would enter and find two eastern lamps still lit, etc. And according to the one who says they were arranged north to south, the middle one had its face turned toward the west, and it

is called the western one, while the rest of the lamps turned their faces toward the middle one, as it is written (Numbers 8), 'toward the face of the lampstand,' meaning the middle one, 'shall the six

lamps give light.' And the fire of the arrangement would grow stronger on its own - it would burn on its own without adding wood, and they did not need to bring wood once they had arranged it in the morning. Except for two

logs - for the afternoon offering, which are obligatory, as stated earlier in this chapter. A curse was sent - meaning, it no longer satisfied him. And every priest's portion was doubled - since it was no longer even an olive's volume,

once they saw that it did not satisfy, the modest ones would withdraw their hands (though if there was extra, they would not withdraw their hands), whereas in Shimon's days, whoever received a doubled portion, they would not withdraw their hands.

Chometzan - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment (identifying the word as meaning 'a robber,' opening a new discussion of the verse 'God rescued me from the hand of the wicked, from the grip of the wrongdoer') continues on 39b.
